_note: Moon counts change as new discoveries are confirmed. Values below are as of moonsAsOf. Check science.nasa.gov before publishing.

sun.overview: The Sun holds 99.86% of all the mass in the solar system.
sun.funFact: Sunlight takes 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth. You never see the Sun as it is now, only as it was.

mercury.overview: The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. It has almost no atmosphere to hold heat, so it swings between scorching and frozen more violently than anywhere else in the solar system.
mercury.funFact: One solar day on Mercury (sunrise to sunrise) lasts 176 Earth days, which is two full Mercury years. The planet completes two orbits between one dawn and the next.

venus.overview: Nearly Earth's twin in size, and nothing like it otherwise. A runaway greenhouse effect has left the surface hot enough to melt lead, under pressure equivalent to a kilometre beneath Earth's ocean.
venus.funFact: A day on Venus is longer than its year, and it spins backwards! The Sun rises in the west and sets in the east.

earth.overview: The only place known to have liquid water on its surface, plate tectonics, and life. Its large moon stabilises its axial tilt, which keeps the climate steadier than it would otherwise be.
earth.funFact: Earth is the densest planet in the solar system, and the only one whose name doesn't come from Greek or Roman mythology.

mars.overview: A cold desert world with a day almost exactly as long as Earth's. Its thin atmosphere and rusted iron surface give it the red colour visible to the naked eye.
mars.funFact: Olympus Mons is 22 km tall (roughly two and a half Everests!) It's so wide that standing on it, the slope would be gentle enough that you might not notice you were on a mountain.

jupiter.overview: More massive than every other planet combined, twice over. Jupiter has no surface: the atmosphere simply thickens with depth until hydrogen behaves like a liquid metal.
jupiter.funFact: The Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has been under continuous observation since the 1600s. It is currently shrinking.

saturn.overview: The least dense planet in the solar system, wrapped in the most spectacular ring system. The rings are made almost entirely of water ice and may be younger than the dinosaurs.
saturn.funFact: Saturn's density is 0.687 g/cm³. Drop it in a large enough ocean and it would float. The rings span 280,000 km but average only about 10 metres thick.

uranus.overview: Knocked onto its side, most likely by an ancient collision. Uranus orbits the Sun lying down, which gives it the strangest seasons of any planet.
uranus.funFact: Tilted 98°, each pole gets 42 years of continuous sunlight followed by 42 years of darkness. It also holds the record for the coldest temperature measured in the solar system: -224 °C.

neptune.overview: The most distant planet, and the only one found by mathematics before anyone looked at it. Irregularities in Uranus's orbit pointed straight to where it had to be.

stats.Discovered: Urbain Le Verrier and Johann Galle, 1846

neptune.funFact: Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system, reaching 2,100 km/h. It has completed only one full orbit since its discovery, in 2011.
